subject: Geography
description: Mountains, deserts, oceans, plateaus — world extremes & famous superlatives

questions.stem: The HIGHEST peak in the world is:

options.option_text: Mount Kilimanjaro
Mount Everest
K2
Kangchenjunga

questions.explanation: Mount Everest — 8,848.86 m (newly measured 2020). K2 is second (8,611 m). Kangchenjunga is third (8,586 m) and the highest in India. Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) is Africa's highest. Everest is on Nepal-Tibet border.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The LARGEST desert in the world (by area) is:

options.option_text: Sahara
Antarctica
Gobi
Thar

questions.explanation: Antarctica is technically a polar desert (very low precipitation) covering ~14.2 million sq km — the largest desert. Sahara (~9.2 million sq km) is the largest HOT desert. Desert definition: <25 cm annual precipitation.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Match the OCEAN/SEA with its LOCATION-FACT. A. Pacific Ocean.  B. Atlantic Ocean.  C. Indian Ocean.  D. Arctic Ocean. List-II: 1. World's largest and deepest (Mariana Trench).  2. S-shaped; separates Americas from Europe/Africa.  3. Only ocean named after a country.  4. Smallest ocean, frozen most of the year.
questions.explanation: Pacific — largest (~165 million km²), deepest point = Challenger Deep in Mariana Trench (10,994 m). Atlantic — S-shape. Indian — only ocean named for a country. Arctic — smallest (~14 million km²), mostly frozen.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The IMAGINARY line at 0° longitude passing through Greenwich is called:

options.option_text: Tropic of Cancer
Prime Meridian
International Date Line
Equator

questions.explanation: Prime Meridian — 0° longitude, passes through Greenwich, London. Equator — 0° latitude (dividing N/S hemispheres). Tropic of Cancer — 23.5° N. International Date Line — approximately 180° longitude (zig-zags to avoid splitting countries).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: 'ROOF OF THE WORLD' is a term often used for:

options.option_text: Himalayas
Pamir Knot / Plateau
Tibetan Plateau (sometimes also used for this)
Andes

questions.explanation: The Pamir Mountains ('Pamir Knot', intersection of Hindu Kush, Karakoram, Kunlun, Tian Shan, Himalayas) is traditionally called the 'Roof of the World'. The Tibetan Plateau is also often given this epithet — both are acceptable in Indian exam context; Pamir is the more classical answer.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which is the DEEPEST lake in the world?

options.option_text: Caspian Sea (actually a lake)
Lake Baikal
Lake Tanganyika
Dead Sea

questions.explanation: Lake Baikal (Siberia, Russia) — maximum depth 1,642 m, the deepest and one of the oldest (~25 million years). Caspian Sea is the LARGEST lake by area. Dead Sea — lowest elevation lake (~430 m below sea level).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The HIGHEST waterfall in the world is:

options.option_text: Niagara Falls
Angel Falls (Venezuela)
Victoria Falls
Iguazu Falls

questions.explanation: Angel Falls (Salto Ángel), Venezuela — 979 m total drop — world's highest uninterrupted waterfall. Victoria Falls (Zambia/Zimbabwe) is widest+highest-flow. Niagara (USA/Canada) is most popular tourist. Iguazu (Brazil/Argentina) has the broadest spread.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The 'Ring of Fire', associated with roughly 75% of the world's active volcanoes and about 90% of major earthquakes, encircles which ocean?

options.option_text: The Atlantic Ocean, along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge system
The Indian Ocean, from the African to Australian coasts
The Pacific Ocean, encircling its entire eastern and western rim
The Arctic Ocean, running along the northern polar boundary

questions.explanation: The Ring of Fire is a horseshoe-shaped belt of seismic and volcanic activity around the Pacific Ocean's perimeter, stretching from New Zealand through Japan, the Philippines, and the Americas. The Atlantic has the Mid-Atlantic Ridge with some volcanic activity, but its intensity is far below the Pacific — making it the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.stem: Which mountain range forms the traditional geographic boundary between Europe and Asia, running from the Arctic Ocean southward into Kazakhstan?

options.option_text: The Ural Mountains, extending from Arctic to Kazakhstan
The Caucasus Mountains, separating the Black and Caspian Seas
The Alps Mountains, running through the heart of central Europe
The Carpathian Mountains, curving through Eastern Europe broadly

questions.explanation: The Ural Mountains mark the conventional Europe-Asia boundary, along with the Ural River and Caspian Sea. The Caucasus Mountains are a common distractor because they also straddle the boundary further south — but geographers treat the Urals as the primary accepted dividing line. The Alps are entirely within Europe.

questions.stem: The Strait of Malacca, one of the world's most strategically critical shipping lanes carrying over a quarter of global trade, lies between which two landmasses?

options.option_text: The islands of Sumatra and Java, both part of Indonesia
Malay Peninsula and the island of Borneo to its east
Southern Thailand and the northwestern tip of Sri Lanka
Malay Peninsula and the island of Sumatra, Indonesia

questions.explanation: The Strait of Malacca runs between the Malay Peninsula (Malaysia, Singapore, southern Thailand) and the Indonesian island of Sumatra. The Sunda Strait (between Sumatra and Java) is the most common confusion. Borneo lies to the east in the South China Sea and does not border this strait at all.

questions.stem: The theory of 'Continental Drift' — proposing that Earth's continents were once joined in a single supercontinent — was first systematically framed by which scientist?

options.option_text: Charles Darwin, using biological evolution and fossil patterns
Alfred Wegener, using coastline fit and matching fossil records
Harry Hess, based on seafloor spreading and ocean ridge data
Edward Suess, based on rock formation links across continents

questions.explanation: Alfred Wegener proposed Continental Drift in 1912 using matching coastlines (especially South America and Africa), identical fossils on now-separated continents, and similar rock strata. Harry Hess later proposed seafloor spreading (1960s), which provided the physical mechanism. Edward Suess coined 'Gondwana' and 'Tethys Sea' but did not frame the drift theory systematically.

questions.stem: The Great Barrier Reef — the world's largest coral reef system and a UNESCO World Heritage Site — lies off the coast of which Australian state or territory?

options.option_text: New South Wales coast, along southeastern Australia
Western Australia, along its lengthy southwestern coastline
Queensland, along the northeastern coast of Australia
Northern Territory, along Australia's tropical north coast

questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 km along Queensland's northeastern coast in the Coral Sea. Northern Territory is the most tempting distractor because of its tropical location — but the reef specifically runs along Queensland. It is the world's largest living structure and is visible from space.

questions.stem: The 'Foehn' is a warm, dry wind descending the leeward slopes of the Alps in Europe. Which wind in the Rocky Mountains of North America is its meteorological equivalent, locally nicknamed for causing rapid snowmelt?

options.option_text: Chinook wind, locally nicknamed the 'snow eater' in Rockies
Mistral wind, descending cold through the Rhône Valley, France
Sirocco wind, blowing hot and dusty from Sahara into Europe
Harmattan wind, carrying dust off the Sahara into West Africa

questions.explanation: The Chinook is a warm, dry föhn-type wind descending the eastern slopes of the Rockies, nicknamed 'snow eater' for dramatically melting snow in hours. The Mistral is cold, not warm, and blows down France's Rhône Valley — not North America. Sirocco and Harmattan are both Saharan-origin hot winds entirely unrelated to the Rocky Mountain system.

questions.stem: The seismic discontinuity at approximately 2,900 km depth — where S-waves disappear and P-wave velocity drops sharply, marking the boundary between the silicate mantle and the liquid iron-nickel outer core — is named which discontinuity?

options.option_text: The Lehmann Discontinuity, at the inner and outer core interface
The Conrad Discontinuity, separating upper from lower crust zone
The Gutenberg Discontinuity, between the mantle and outer core
The Mohorovičić Discontinuity, at the crust and upper mantle

questions.explanation: The Gutenberg Discontinuity (core-mantle boundary, CMB) at ~2,891 km is where S-waves cannot pass (liquid outer core blocks shear waves) and P-waves slow sharply. The Moho (Mohorovičić) marks the crust-mantle boundary at 5–70 km; Lehmann marks the outer/inner core boundary at ~5,100 km; Conrad separates upper from lower crust — all four are classic exam mix-up targets.
